## Scope

The field of gas drying is one that has attracted a great deal of research attention over the years, and adsorbents sit right at the heart of a wide range of drying processes across industry. Gas streams have to be dried for all sorts of reasons: water vapour left in a gas can condense in cold pipework, corrode equipment, form solid hydrates that block lines, or interfere with a downstream process that expects a dry feed, and in application after application, from natural gas leaving a wellhead to the instrument air that drives plant control systems, it is adsorbents that are called upon to remove that water. This review sets out to survey the literature on adsorbents for gas drying, taking in the three great families of materials that dominate the area in practice: silica gel, activated alumina, and zeolite molecular sieves. In total, the review covers 128 papers published over the last 13 years, which together provide a rich and varied picture of a field that continues to evolve. The review is organised into four parts, moving from the scope of the literature, through the results that can be regarded as firmly established, to the areas where different research groups disagree with one another, and finally to the gaps where further work is sorely needed.

## Established results

A number of findings have emerged again and again across the literature and can now be treated as firmly established. All three families of adsorbent are capable of drying gas streams effectively, and each has found its established place in industrial practice. Silica gel and activated alumina are widely used where the drying duty is moderate, while molecular sieves are the materials of choice where very dry gas is required, since they continue to take up water strongly even when the gas is already quite dry and even at elevated temperatures, conditions under which the other materials lose much of their capacity. It is also well established that these adsorbents are used in cycles: a bed takes up water until it approaches saturation, and it is then regenerated, typically by heating it or by passing a dry purge gas through it, so that it can be returned to service. In practice this cyclic character is commonly managed by arranging beds in pairs or in groups, so that while one bed is on stream drying the gas, another is being regenerated, and the two exchange roles on a regular switching cycle that keeps the drying duty continuous. The regeneration step is every bit as much a part of the process as the adsorption step, and the conditions under which it is carried out, the temperature reached, the purge used, and the completeness with which the bed is dried back, all have a bearing on the performance that follows. The broad pattern of behaviour, in other words, is not in doubt, and the literature speaks with a largely consistent voice on these fundamentals.

## Disagreements

Beneath that settled surface, however, there are important areas where the published reports do not agree with one another, and chief among these is the quantity of water uptake reported at low water vapour concentrations in the gas. Different groups, studying what are nominally very similar materials under apparently similar conditions, have published values that differ from one another by margins far larger than the uncertainties the individual studies themselves suggest. This is a frustrating state of affairs for anyone who wishes to design a dryer on the basis of the published data, because the low-concentration uptake is precisely the quantity that governs how dry the gas leaving the bed will ultimately be. A careful reading of the conflicting reports suggests that the divergence has a great deal to do with the way the measurements were made: some groups measured uptake directly by weighing the adsorbent, while others inferred it from breakthrough behaviour, and the activation and pretreatment of the samples before measurement also varied considerably from study to study, which can shift the results significantly. On top of this, the studies differ in the form of material tested, some working with fine powders and others with the formed pellets and beads that are actually loaded into industrial vessels, and in how long the sample was left in contact with the humid gas before the measurement was taken, a detail that matters greatly where uptake is slow to settle at low concentrations. The humidity of the test gas itself was generated and controlled in different ways, adding yet another layer of variation that is difficult to unpick after the event. Until these methodological questions are ironed out, the disagreement on this quantity is likely to persist.

## Gaps

Finally, there are striking gaps in the literature where measurements that ought to exist simply have not been reported at all. The most notable of these concerns what happens to an adsorbent over the long term in real cyclic service. Study after study reports the uptake of a fresh sample, carefully activated and measured under clean laboratory conditions, yet the measurement that nobody seems to report is how the capacity of the same material holds up after it has been put through repeated adsorption and regeneration cycles, one after another, as it would be in any real plant. Closely related to this is the near-absence of reporting on the regeneration side of the cycle: many studies are vague about the exact conditions used to dry their samples back between measurements, which makes it hard to know whether the material being measured in one laboratory is in the same state as the material measured in another. Alongside this, the effects of trace contaminants in industrial gas streams, which are largely absent from laboratory feeds, are seldom followed over time, even though in service it is often contamination rather than water itself that slowly degrades a bed. There is also a scale question that the literature largely steps around, in that nearly all measurements are made on small samples under carefully controlled conditions, while the behaviour of a full industrial bed, with its flow distribution and its temperature fronts, is inferred rather than observed. These gaps matter enormously, because a dryer is not bought for its first cycle but for years of cycling, and the literature, for all its richness, leaves the designer largely guessing on precisely the questions that service life depends upon.

## Scope

This review covers adsorbents for gas drying: silica gel, activated alumina, and zeolite molecular sieves, the three material classes in industrial use for removing water vapour from gas streams. The duties behind the literature are consistent: water left in a gas condenses in cold pipework, corrodes steel, forms solid hydrates that block lines, and enters downstream processes that require a dry feed. Natural gas, instrument air, and process gas feeds are the recurring applications, and the adsorbent bed is the standard means of drying all three. The review draws on 128 papers from the last 13 years. It reports first what the literature establishes, then the quantity on which reports conflict, and finally the measurement the literature does not contain.

## Established results

The literature reports the outcome of a drying duty as the water content, or the dew point, of the treated gas, and reports the adsorbent side of the duty as an uptake: the mass of water the material takes up under stated conditions. Uptake is the quantity the sections below keep returning to, because it is the quantity from which bed size, cycle time, and the dryness reached are all worked out. Where a report gives the one without the conditions that produced it, the figure cannot be carried to another duty.

The three classes all dry gas, and their ordering by duty is settled. Silica gel and activated alumina carry the moderate duties. Molecular sieves carry the duties where very dry gas is required: a molecular sieve keeps taking up water at low water vapour concentrations, and at temperatures, where silica gel and activated alumina have lost most of their capacity. That behaviour is reported consistently enough, across enough independent groups, to be treated as established.

The mode of operation is likewise settled. An adsorbent bed takes up water until it approaches saturation and is then regenerated, by heating or by a dry purge gas, and returned to service. Industrial dryers arrange this as a switching cycle, with one bed drying the gas while another regenerates, so the duty is continuous although each bed alternates. Regeneration is part of the duty, not a pause in it: the temperature the bed is taken to, the purge it is swept with, and the dryness it is brought back to together set the state from which the next adsorption step starts. Drying on these materials is a cyclic process in every industrial application the review covers, and comparisons between materials are comparisons between cycles, not between single passes. Fresh-sample capacity is therefore a property of the first cycle only, a point the gaps section returns to.

## Disagreements

Reports conflict on the water uptake of these materials at low water vapour concentrations. Groups studying nominally similar materials under nominally similar conditions publish values that stand apart by more than the uncertainty any of the studies claims for itself. The conflict cannot be settled from the published values, because the values were not measured the same way. It matters because low-concentration uptake is the property that sets how dry the treated gas can be made: the contested quantity is the design quantity.

Weighing the conflicting reports against their test conditions points to method as the source. Some groups measured uptake directly, by weighing the adsorbent; others inferred uptake from breakthrough curves, a route that folds the dynamics of the test bed into the figure reported as capacity. Pretreatment differed as well: the activation of the sample before measurement, which sets the state the measurement starts from, was neither uniform nor always reported in full. The form of the sample differed, powder in some studies and formed pellets in others, and formed material presents its water with a longer path into each particle. Contact time differed too, and at low vapour concentrations uptake settles slowly, so a measurement closed early reports a value still on its way to equilibrium. The humidity of the test gas was generated by different means in different laboratories, with different control over the concentration that the whole measurement depends on. A disagreement produced by method is not evidence about the materials, and the review treats the low-concentration uptake of all three classes as unsettled until the measurements are made on a common basis.

A further share of the conflict sits in the materials themselves. A class name is not a material specification: silica gels, aluminas, and molecular sieves from different makers differ in binder, in forming, and in pore structure, and two samples carrying the same class name can be measurably different adsorbents. Reports that name the class and not the maker, or the maker and not the grade, leave the reader unable to tell a method difference from a material difference, and part of the published spread is likely to be exactly that confusion, recorded as if it were a property of the class.

## Gaps

The measurement nobody reports is the change in capacity over repeated cycles. The literature characterises fresh samples: activated, clean, measured once. A dryer in service adsorbs and is regenerated cycle after cycle, and its working capacity after many cycles is the figure a design actually spends. That figure is absent. Reports do not follow one sample through repeated regeneration under stated conditions and report the capacity it retains.

Two neighbouring absences compound the first. The regeneration conditions used between measurements are themselves often reported loosely, so the state of the material at the start of one group's measurement cannot be matched to the state in another's; and the trace contaminants present in industrial gas, absent from laboratory feeds, are not followed over time, although in service it is contamination as much as water that ages a bed. The published measurements are also made on small samples under controlled flow, and the step from sample behaviour to the behaviour of a full bed, with its flow distribution and moving temperature fronts, is taken by inference in every design the review covers.

The gap is structural, not incidental: a cycling study takes far longer than a fresh-sample study and produces a less quotable result. Its absence nonetheless fixes the scope of every claim the literature supports. What is established is how these adsorbents behave when new; how they behave in the service they are bought for is, on the published record, unmeasured.
